followUps:
ReadyToRun precompiles IL to native code ahead of time but still uses the JIT for tuning; Native AOT compiles everything to a native executable and drops the JIT.

ReadyToRun code is not fully optimised, so hot methods are later re-JITted at tier 1. It cuts startup time and needs the runtime installed. Native AOT gives the fastest start and least memory, but no Assembly.Load, no Reflection.Emit, limited reflection, and larger per-platform builds.

The first request pays one-time costs that later requests do not: JIT compiling the code paths, loading assemblies, building the DI container and route tables, opening connections and warming caches.

Example: the first call might take 300 ms because 2,000 methods are compiled at tier 0, while the hundredth takes 5 ms. Fixes: ReadyToRun, a warm-up request at startup, and tiered PGO. Native AOT removes the JIT cost entirely.

.NET Standard was a versioned contract of APIs that several runtimes (Framework, Core, Xamarin) all implemented, so one library could be shared among them. Today it is mostly not needed.

Since .NET 5 there is one runtime family, so a library should simply target net8.0 (or net8.0;net48 if Framework consumers remain). Only use netstandard2.0 when you must support old Framework apps and cannot multi-target. Version 2.1 never ran on Framework at all.

Migrate in small steps, starting with the libraries nothing else depends on, and keep tests green at each step.

  1. Run the .NET Upgrade Assistant and the API analyser to find unsupported APIs.
  2. Convert the old .csproj to SDK style and PackageReference.
  3. Multi-target net48;net8.0 so both old and new apps can consume it.
  4. Replace Windows-only pieces (registry, WCF client, System.Web) or use compatibility packages.
  5. Drop net48 when the last consumer has moved.

code.title: Value types copy, reference types share

followUps:
It lives on the heap, not the stack, because the compiler hoists captured variables into a hidden class (a closure object).

For int n = 0; Action a = () => n++; the compiler generates a class with a field n and your method uses that field. The closure object is allocated once per scope entry and kept alive as long as the delegate is. In a hot loop this costs an allocation; static lambdas or passing state explicitly avoid it.

Because strings can be large and have a variable length, so they must be stored as an object on the heap with a reference to it, not copied whole on every assignment.

Copying a 1 MB string by value on each method call would be very slow, while copying an 8-byte reference is cheap. Immutability makes this safe: nobody can change the shared text, so strings can be shared, cached (interning) and used as dictionary keys. The price is that s += x in a loop creates a new string each time, so use StringBuilder there.

code.title: decimal is exact, double drifts

followUps:
By default Math.Round on a decimal uses banker's rounding: a value exactly halfway goes to the nearest even digit. Pass a MidpointRounding mode to choose something else.

Math.Round(2.5m) is 2, Math.Round(3.5m) is 4, but Math.Round(2.5m, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero) is 3. Most invoices and tax rules want AwayFromZero. Also round once at the end, not on every step, or small errors add up.

Use decimal (for example DECIMAL(19,4) or NUMERIC(12,2)), never float, because float is binary and stores 0.1 only approximately.

Summing 0.10 ten thousand times in float gives something like 999.9999999 and the cents will not match a ledger. A fixed-scale decimal column stores exact digits, makes SUM exact, and maps cleanly to C# decimal. Another option is storing integer cents in a bigint, which is also exact.

code.title: Unchecked wraps, checked throws

followUps:
Very little in the usual case: a checked add compiles to a normal add plus a jump-on-overflow check, so it costs about a branch that is almost never taken.

Measured in tight loops it is typically a few percent slower, because it can stop the JIT from vectorising or reordering. For business code it is negligible, so using checked for money or sizes is a cheap safety net. Profile first before turning it off in hot numeric kernels.

No. checked and unchecked affect only the arithmetic written lexically inside the block or expression, not the methods it calls.

int F(int a) => a + 1;   // uses the project default
checked { int x = F(int.MaxValue); }  // F still wraps

To make a whole method checked, put the operations inside checked(...) there, or set CheckForOverflowUnderflow for the whole project.

code.title: const vs readonly vs static readonly

followUps:
Expose it through an immutable or read-only type, because readonly alone only stops reassigning the field.

Options: ImmutableArray<T> or ImmutableList<T> (cannot change at all), IReadOnlyList<T> or ReadOnlyCollection<T> (a read-only view; the owner can still change the inner list), or FrozenDictionary for lookups. Return copies or views from public members, not the raw mutable collection.

Yes, in most cases: reflection can write a readonly instance field, though it is a bad idea and the behaviour is not guaranteed.

Static readonly fields of primitives may already have been inlined by the JIT as constants, so your change is silently ignored. const cannot be changed because it is baked into the caller code. Treat it as unsupported; use a mutable field or a settings object if a value must change.

code.title: var is static typing, not dynamic

followUps:
Target-typed new (C# 9) lets you leave out the type on the right when the left side already states it: List<int> xs = new();.

It is the mirror image of var: with var the type is on the right, with new() it is on the left. It is nice for fields (private readonly Dictionary<string,int> _map = new();) and arguments. It does not work with var because there is nothing to infer from.

Since C# 10 the compiler infers a delegate type for a lambda, usually Func<...> or Action<...>, when the types are clear; before that it was an error.

var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;   // Func<int,int,int>
var hi = () => Console.WriteLine("hi"); // Action
var bad = x => x + 1;  // error: x has no type

Parameter types must be written, because there is nothing else to infer them from.

code.title: Culture changes number parsing and output

followUps:
It is a runtime setting (InvariantGlobalization=true) that turns off ICU/NLS culture data, so all cultures behave like the invariant culture and no ICU library is needed.

It makes Docker images smaller (no libicu) and startup slightly faster. The catch: culture-specific formatting, sorting and casing (for example Turkish I) no longer happens, and creating some cultures can throw. Good for backend services using only invariant formats; wrong for apps that show localised text.

Pass a StringComparison to every comparison: Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase for identifiers, paths and protocols.

string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
a.StartsWith("http", StringComparison.Ordinal);

Ordinal compares raw char values, so it is fast and gives the same result on every machine. Use InvariantCulture only for sorting that must be linguistic yet stable, and CurrentCulture for text a user sees.

code.title: Fast integer input with a byte buffer

followUps:
Handle a leading minus sign by setting a flag and negating at the end, and treat both \r and \n as separators because every byte at or below a space is whitespace.

if (b == '-') neg = true;
else if (b > ' ') v = v * 10 + (b - '0');
else if (any) break;   // \r, \n, ' ', tab end a number
result = neg ? -v : v;

So "-14\r\n15" gives -14 and 15 with no special CRLF code.

Output written to a buffered StreamWriter may never appear, or only partly, because the data is still sitting in memory when the program exits.

With AutoFlush = false you must call Flush() or dispose the writer (using) before exit. A typical bug: the first 64 KB show up and the rest is lost, or on a judge the answer is empty. Console.Out itself auto-flushes, which is why it is slower with 106 lines.

Put the public entry-point logic in a type the test can reach, or make the generated Program class visible to the test project.

Top-level statements generate an internal Program class. Add public partial class Program { } at the bottom of the file (or InternalsVisibleTo), then use WebApplicationFactory<Program> from Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing to start the app in memory and call it with an HttpClient.

The compiler reports an error, because it cannot tell which one is the entry point, unless you choose one explicitly.

Set <StartupObject>MyApp.Tools.Program</StartupObject> in the project file (or the /main compiler option) to name the class. Without that, error CS0017 "more than one entry point" is raised. Overloads of Main with other signatures are ignored; only valid entry-point signatures count.

Logging needs a constant message template so that the message can be grouped and searched, and so that formatting is skipped if the level is off.

logger.LogInformation("User {Id} paid {Amount}", id, amt) keeps Id and Amount as separate fields and the template as one stable key. An interpolated string builds a different text every time, so you cannot group by it, and it may allocate before the level check. Use the logger's templates or source-generated [LoggerMessage].

string.Create builds a string of a known length directly in its final memory, avoiding temporary strings, and the interpolated overload also takes a culture.

string s = string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
    $"{price:F2} USD");

The IFormatProvider parameter makes numbers and dates format with a chosen culture instead of the current one, so the same code is safe for files and protocols. It also writes into a pooled buffer, so there is one final allocation.

code.title: Casts truncate, Round uses banker's rounding

followUps:
Math.Floor(-3.7) is -4, because floor rounds toward negative infinity, the next whole number below.

Compare the four ways to round -3.7: truncate ((int)) gives -3, Floor gives -4, Ceiling gives -3, Round gives -4. For positive numbers truncate and floor are the same, which is why the difference surprises people only with negatives. Note that Floor returns a double, so a cast is needed to get an int.

They are extra MidpointRounding options (added in .NET Core 3.0) for exact halves: ToZero drops the half toward zero, ToNegativeInfinity rounds down, and ToPositiveInfinity rounds up.

Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.ToZero);             // 2
Math.Round(-2.5, MidpointRounding.ToNegativeInfinity); // -3
Math.Round(-2.5, MidpointRounding.ToPositiveInfinity); // -2

They only matter for exact midpoints; all other values round to the nearest.

code.title: Overflow-safe int multiply without long

followUps:
The CPU sets an overflow flag (OF) in its status register when a signed add or multiply result does not fit; the carry flag does the same for unsigned.

Example with 8 bits: 100 + 100 = 200 does not fit in -128..127, so the result wraps to -56 and OF is set. C# checked code emits a jump-on-overflow (jo) after the operation; unchecked code ignores the flag. For multiplication, x86 imul sets the same flag.

They convert one numeric type to another with a chosen policy for values that do not fit: CreateChecked throws, CreateSaturating clamps to the limit, and CreateTruncating wraps like a plain cast.

int.CreateChecked(300L);         // 300
byte.CreateSaturating(300);      // 255
byte.CreateTruncating(300);      // 44
byte.CreateChecked(300);         // OverflowException

They come from generic math (.NET 7) and work in generic code via INumberBase<T>.

Anything that uses reflection to find types at run time, because trimming and AOT remove code that nothing refers to statically.

Typical breakages: reflection-based JSON serialisers (use source-generated System.Text.Json), older DI containers, ORMs that build queries by reflection, and Assembly.Load plugin systems. The linker cannot see Type.GetType("Foo") so it deletes Foo, causing a crash only at run time. Use the analyser warnings (IL2026, IL3050) and [DynamicallyAccessedMembers].

Dynamic PGO is a runtime that learns from the running program, while AOT decides everything before it starts, so for long-running services PGO usually reaches higher peak speed.

The JIT instruments hot methods, then recompiles them using what it saw: the real hot paths, inlining of the most common virtual call target, and fast paths for likely types. AOT cannot see real traffic. The trade is warm-up: JIT is slow for the first seconds, AOT is fast immediately. Use AOT for short-lived tools, JIT for steady servers.
